children: Emma Tucker
1. FROM MY DESK

This summer, when the U.S. and Iran signed a temporary truce, China touted its role in easing tensions in the Middle East. That same day, a plane from China landed in Tehran carrying electronics components that can be used to make parts for drones and missile guidance systems, according to Iranian customs data analyzed by the Journal.

Two days later, there were more than a dozen other shipments carrying parts worth more than $6 million that can be used in drones. Chinese entities have made thousands of shipments of such "dual use" tech.

Chinese leader Xi Jinping is visiting President Trump in Washington this week for a summit covering weighty topics including trade, artificial intelligence and Taiwan. But the elephant in the room will be China's continuing support for Iran.

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you're not subscribed, sign up here. If you're reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.
2. TODAY'S HEADLINES

A federal judge ordered Trump to temporarily restore White House access for CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists, days after the news organizations were banned over their coverage of the administration.

Venezuelan leader Delcy Rodríguez hailed a national "rebirth" in an address to the U.N. General Assembly and said elections would be held but offered no details on when or how a democratic transition would take place.
An OpenAI agent infiltrated a government-services website in Australia this summer, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said.
Meta Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg announced a new hand-held AI device and other tech products he said take consumers closer to "personal superintelligence."
Oil executives and their lobbyists launched a coordinated contingency plan to persuade the Trump administration not to enact a ban on U.S. diesel exports.
Democrats backed an independent in Nebraska. Leaked tapes make him a risky bet.
3. LIVE FROM THE MARKETS
Follow our live financial coverage all day.

Stocks Spencer Jakab is watching: McDonald's was riding high just seven months ago with its stock price at a record. But the Iran war's effects have been tough for the Golden Arches. Now, after McDonald's announced a plan Wednesday to spend billions sprucing up its beleaguered franchisees' restaurants, the stock has had its biggest drop since last year's Liberation Day swoon and is down more than 30% from that February high. A perfect storm is raging in the bond market.

4. READ IT HERE FIRST
The AI build-out is becoming the biggest economic bet in U.S. history.

Total investment in data centers and related AI infrastructure is projected to be $10.3 trillion from 2025 to 2032, according to new estimates by economist Stijn van Nieuwerburgh published by the Brookings Institution. That is a staggering 3.6% of gross domestic product a year, on average. Never before has the U.S. economy been so dependent on the build-out of a single industry. The investment is transforming every corner of the economy, creating hundreds of thousands of jobs and minting new billionaires. It is also creating significant risk, as much of it is built on debt. An abrupt slowdown could ignite shock waves throughout the U.S. economy, report Konrad Putzier and Justin Lahart.
There's a group chat where world leaders are racing to create AI controls. Texts between the leaders of Canada, France and Norway reveal an emerging alliance.
5. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK

Computational journalist Brian Whitton: In the early spring, I got together with my colleagues on the data team to answer a key question driving our midterms coverage: What could online conversations tell us about what voters care about ahead of the election?

We spent the next several months building an AI tool that consumes content from across the digital world. It worked a little too well. We've got thousands of hours of cable news broadcasts, a quarter million podcast episodes and over 11 million TikToks.
Making sense of it all is a challenge. We've spent endless hours reading transcripts and watching hours of TikToks to fact-check the tool's findings.

One thing we're interested in is how nonpolitical ideas are characterized in political spaces. We think there's more to say about how ideology and politics move through spaces we haven't traditionally had a pulse on.

We're planning a series of reports based on what the tool surfaces between now and Election Day. This first dispatch focused on podcasts, and how the conversation among Trump's most vocal supporters has changed since the 2024 election, when MAGA podcasts really set the agenda.

One of the biggest surprises to us was also the most basic: The tool actually worked. It made it easy to click around and find ordinary creators posting political content. Over the summer, we started to see it in glimmers-a New Age spirituality influencer launching into a tirade on data centers, a skincare-deals account weighing in on Mitch McConnell's health and a tech reviewer lamenting the effect of tariffs.

Another unexpected finding was how much the Lindsay Clancy trial showed up in the MAGA podcast universe. It was popular among both political commentators and nonpolitical creators alike, from BookTok to fitness bros.

6. SEE THE STORY
Here's how Elon Musk's Sunbelt investments are reshaping his business empire.

More than 20 years after Musk got his start in California, the serial entrepreneur has expanded his empire with infrastructure projects across the southern half of the U.S. This year alone, (Tesla) and (SpaceX) have announced billions of dollars in new projects in Texas and Louisiana. States are racing to offer lucrative tax-incentive packages to win new business from Musk's companies and, in some cases, introducing laws that make it easier for the companies to operate.

8. THE NUMBER
$5 million

That's the price some large cargo ships are paying to pass through the Panama Canal as the Iran war and extreme weather in the Western Hemisphere snarl global trade. The recent bids to use the 50-mile interoceanic waterway, which handles almost 6% of global trade, reflect the canal's crucial role at a time when shipping companies have been forced to shift maritime routes.
9. AND FINALLY...
We've reached peak 'nepo baby.' Every new artist is hit with the label these days.

Call it nepo-baby inflation: A collective obsession with unearthing privilege has broadened the meaning of the term, originally referring to children of A-listers who followed in their parents' footsteps. Now, the label includes emerging stars with any kind of leg up or an air of wealth or status.
